subject: space
title: Solar System Scale
summary: The solar system is overwhelmingly a story of empty space. The Sun is about 109 times wider than Earth, the planets are tiny specks by comparison, and the gaps between them are enormous — the average Earth–Sun distance, one astronomical unit, is about 150 million km. Explore a scale-mode model that toggles between size-only and true-distance views to see why most textbook diagrams quietly compress the distances.

Why diagrams must choose between showing size and showing distance
plainLanguageExplanation: If you drew the solar system on a piece of paper with the planets all visible, you'd be drawing a lie — not on purpose, but because real distances are so huge that the planets would be invisible dots. The Sun is about 109 times wider than Earth. The distance from the Sun to Earth is about 150 million km, and scientists use that distance as a ruler called the astronomical unit (AU). Mercury is about 0.4 AU from the Sun, Jupiter about 5 AU, and Neptune about 30 AU. If you shrank the whole solar system so the Sun was the size of a basketball, Earth would be a peppercorn about 30 m away and Neptune would be a marble nearly a kilometre out. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth and roughly 4–5 hours to reach Neptune. This component's model toggles between two views: a size-only view that lines up the planets like a family photo, and a true-distance view that keeps the sizes honest and pushes the planets far apart — so you can feel the emptiness for yourself.

whyItMatters: Almost every picture of the solar system you've ever seen is a compromise, and understanding that compromise is a real scientific skill: reasoning about scale. Space missions, satellite launches, and even the design of the Voyager probes all depend on engineers holding true distances in their heads. When you learn that the planets are tiny specks in a vast emptiness, questions that seem mysterious — why it takes months to reach Mars, why the outer planets are so cold, why Pluto was demoted to dwarf planet — start answering themselves. Scale is the first big idea that makes the rest of space science click.
scientificName: Relative Scale of the Solar System
tagline: A vast emptiness dotted with specks
didYouKnow: If the Sun were the size of a basketball, the nearest star system, Alpha Centauri, would be another basketball about 7,000 km away — farther than a flight from London to Los Angeles.
compareReason: Scale mode lines the planets up by distance with honest sizes; the Planet Size Comparison component lines them up by size alone — together they separate the two confusions (how big, how far) that diagrams usually blur.
